query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a trace amount of yttrium to the Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA strengthens the adhesion of the protective oxide scale, reducing the rate of degradation under elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing gases and delaying the onset of catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA featuring an fcc matrix with its inherent oxide scale characteristics.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a controlled trace level of yttrium into the alloy composition during the additive manufacturing process.
generation.conditions: Exposure of the alloy to elevated temperatures in oxidizing (and possibly reducing) gas environments, within industrially relevant thermal boundaries.
generation.structural_mediator: The integrity and adhesion of the nanoscale oxide scale at the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: Trace yttrium is hypothesized to segregate to the oxide/alloy interface during high-temperature exposure, modifying the oxide composition and microstructure to enhance its adhesion. This more adherent oxide scale provides better protection against further oxidation and limits stress accumulation that could lead to spallation or catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the starting-state alloy without yttrium, yttrium-doped samples would display a more uniform and adherent oxide layer, lower rates of degradation, and delayed or mitigated catastrophic failure under similar high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
generation.baseline: Performance of the undoped Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA under the same elevated-temperature oxidizing (or reducing) conditions, where less adherent oxide scales lead to faster degradation and higher failure probability.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies primarily to conditions of high temperature in oxidizing environments; its validity in strongly reducing atmospheres remains less certain and would require further investigation.
generation.uncertainty: While prior literature on similar alloys supports yttrium’s beneficial role in oxide-scale adhesion, the specific quantitative improvements in degradation resistance and failure delay for this HEA are not fully determined under all operational conditions. The effect under reducing conditions is also less well established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA specimens: one set with a controlled trace addition of yttrium and one without. Expose both sets to identical high-temperature oxidizing gas environments, monitoring them over time for oxide-scale morphology, thickness, and adhesion as well as overall structural integrity.
measurements: Characterization of the oxide scale (using SEM, TEM, and XPS) for thickness and adhesion quality.
Mechanical testing (e.g., thermal cycling or stress-corrosion cracking tests) to evaluate failure onset.
Monitoring mass change or oxidation kinetics as a function of time.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the yttrium-doped specimens do not show statistically significant improvements in oxide-scale integrity (thickness, adhesion), reduced oxidation rates, or delayed catastrophic failure compared to the undoped specimens under identical conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.

chosen.approach: Trace yttrium addition to improve oxide-scale adhesion in HEAs
